claims.text: Synchronous reduction of all noble-metal precursors causes rapid, simultaneous nucleation.
Simultaneous nucleation and incorporation kinetically freeze a high-entropy alloy structure.
Disrupting the temporal alignment of metal incorporation promotes phase separation or elemental segregation.
The relevant starting material is a well-mixed collection of noble-metal precursors in a single-source solid or solution-based precursor.
Low-temperature reduction conditions limit free atomic mobility.
Under low-mobility conditions, nucleation kinetics are controlled primarily by reduction timing.
Nanoparticle lattice formation during nucleation reflects the degree of atomic mixing.
Concurrent reduction incorporates all constituent metals into nucleating particles at nearly the same time and thereby produces uniform mixing.
Limited atomic mobility kinetically preserves atomic mixing during particle formation.
When reductions are staggered, early-reduced metals initiate nucleation and restrict incorporation of later-reduced metals.
Restriction of later metal incorporation causes phase separation or elemental segregation.
Synchronized reduction produces single-phase HEA nanoparticles with homogeneous elemental distributions.
The nanoparticles produced under synchronized reduction will have high surface area suitable for catalysis.
Altering incorporation timing produces phase separation, elemental segregation, or inhomogeneous morphology.
Naturally balanced reduction kinetics often lead to single-phase HEA nanoparticle formation in multimetal systems.
The proposed synchronization mechanism applies mainly to noble-metal HEA nanoparticle systems containing five or more elements under low-mobility conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in high-temperature regimes with high atomic mobility.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in solution-phase syntheses where precursor diffusion dominates.
The quantitative reduction-rate differences among the individual metals are uncertain.
The temporal-asynchrony threshold required to trigger segregation is uncertain.
